items.label: Research aims
items.prompt: Find the sentence in the INTRODUCTION that states the study's goals.
items.model: (1) How are sleep quality, smartphone dependence and health-related behaviours related in female college students? (2) What predicts sleep quality?
items.why: 'This study had two goals…' gives the aims; the Abstract repeats them.

items.label: Hypothesis
items.prompt: Does this article state a formal hypothesis?
items.model: No. Only goals are stated, followed by a hope about what the results may show.
items.why: 'We hope that the results…' is not a hypothesis; it doesn't predict a specific relationship.

items.label: Variables
items.prompt: What is the dependent (outcome) variable in the regression analyses, and what are the main independent variables?
items.model: DV: sleep quality (good vs poor). IVs: smartphone dependence and health-promoting behaviours (HPLP scores).
items.why: The Statistical analysis section says sleep quality was the dependent variable of the regression model.

items.label: Operational definition (sleep quality)
items.prompt: Find the sentence that names the scale used to measure SLEEP QUALITY.
items.model: The Chinese version of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI); higher scores = worse sleep; >5 = poor sleep.
items.why: The scale is named, then described over several sentences; any of them is accepted.

items.label: Reading the scale
items.prompt: On the PSQI, what does a HIGHER score mean?
items.why: Always check the direction of a scale: on the PSQI, higher = worse. This matters when interpreting negative correlations.

items.label: Operational definition (smartphone dependence)
items.prompt: How was SMARTPHONE DEPENDENCE measured? Find the sentence describing how the items were scored.
items.model: Four items on a 5-point Likert scale (total 4–20); higher = more dependence.
items.why: The items are listed one by one, then the scoring is explained.

items.label: Reliability
items.prompt: What was the Cronbach's alpha for the smartphone dependence measure in this study?
items.why: Cronbach's alpha reports a measure's internal-consistency reliability; values above .70 are usually considered acceptable.

items.label: General method
items.prompt: What general method did this study use?
items.model: Cross-sectional: questionnaires at one point in time.
items.why: The Methods say 'cross-sectional research approach'; nothing was manipulated.

items.label: Sample
items.prompt: How many VALID questionnaires were analysed, and who were the participants?
items.model: 409 female junior college students in southern Taiwan (411 took part; 2 incomplete were excluded).
items.why: Careful: 411 agreed, but only 409 valid questionnaires were analysed.

items.label: Inclusion criteria
items.prompt: Find the sentence giving the INCLUSION criteria.
items.model: Female, had a smartphone for 6+ months, could communicate in Mandarin/Minnan and read Chinese.
items.why: Inclusion criteria say who was allowed to take part; exclusion criteria come in the next sentence.

items.label: Research gap
items.prompt: Find a sentence showing the research gap.
items.model: Most studies focused on negative behaviours, with little attention to how health-PROMOTING behaviours relate to sleep quality.
items.why: Look for 'However, most studies…' or 'they failed to…', which signal what earlier research missed.

items.label: Key result
items.prompt: Find the sentence in the RESULTS reporting which variables PREDICTED sleep quality in the final (stepwise) analysis.
items.model: Smartphone dependence (B = 0.25) and overall HPLP score (B = −0.04) both predicted sleep quality, p < .01.
items.why: The stepwise regression is the last analysis in the Results.

items.label: Overclaiming
items.prompt: The design is cross-sectional, yet one sentence in the CONCLUSIONS uses causal language the design can't support. Find it.
items.model: 'Smartphone usage has great impact on sleep quality…'
items.why: 'Impact' implies cause and effect. The authors themselves admit in the limitations that they cannot infer cause.

items.label: Limitation (self-report)
items.prompt: The limitations are numbered First, Second, Finally. Find the FIRST limitation.
items.model: All data were self-reported, so recall bias may have occurred.
items.why: The first limitation is about how data were collected.

items.label: Limitation (sample)
items.prompt: Find the limitation about the SAMPLE.
items.model: All participants came from the same school, so conclusions must be conservative (limited generalisability).
items.why: 'Same school' limits how far the findings can be generalised.

items.label: Future research
items.prompt: Find the suggestion for future research.
items.why: It comes right after the design limitation, which it is meant to fix.

items.label: Practical implication
items.prompt: Find a sentence giving a practical recommendation for improving students' sleep.
items.model: Encourage students to cultivate self-affirmation, a positive attitude, good relationships and stress management.
items.why: Practical implications tell people what to DO; here they are written as recommendations rather than labelled 'implications'.
